# First, identify the depth of the soil compaction layer. According to Dr. Gary C. Steinhardt, Purdue University, "to minimize or correct soil compaction you need to …identify the nature and extent of the problem in the field,” (Steinhardt 1985). There are two methods to determine the presence of soil compaction and depth of the compaction layer or tillage pan. These procedures work best when soil is moist to the touch below the surface. # One way is to dig a hole and observe the soil structure for compacted, platy soil layers. Dig a hole two feet deep and look for wormholes and old root channels. With a strong bladed knife stuck 3- inches deep in the sidewall near the bottom of the hole, slowly pull the knife up until it is nearly impossible to lift higher. Your hand will feel resistance. This is the bottom of a compaction pan. Determine the depth of the pan by following the same procedure from the soil surface. A second way is to use a soil penetrometer. This is thin rod with a spring-loaded gage that records the pressure needed to penetrate the soil. Push the penetrometer slowly into the soil until it reads 300 PSI or more. Stop and measure the depth. Then push the penetrometer deeper until it reads less than 300 PSI. Note the depth. This method determines the width and depth of soil compaction and works best when soil moisture is at Field Capacity. # Determine Soil Moisture Conditions –Plastic Limit Plastic limit is the soil moisture content at which soil material can be deformed without rupture or soil particles start to slide over each other. At or above (wetter than) the plastic limit significant soil compaction will occur. Below (drier than) the plastic limit minimal compaction will occur. “Soils with AWC at or above field capacity have the greatest potential for compaction. Water acts as a lubricant between soil particles that allows soil to be pushed together. As more air space is replaced with water, the potential for compaction increases up to a maximum point referred to as the “plastic limit.” At soil saturation levels above the plastic limit the compaction potential of the topsoil declines since water can’t be compressed. This results in the compaction force being directly transferred to the subsoil, increasing the risk of subsoil compaction.” (Duiker, 1994). 1. Take about 1 tablespoon of soil, enough soil to make a 1/8 in. (3 mm) rod (rope, thread, wire) between fingers and palms with little or no rod extending outside of fingers or palms. 2. Squeeze and form the soil into an ellipsoidal-shape mass. 3. Roll this mass between the fingers or palms with just enough pressure to roll the mass into a rod of uniform diameter along its length. Roll out between 40 and 45 strokes per 30 seconds, counting a stroke as one back and forth motion. The sample must be rolled into the 1/8 in. (3 mm) rod in about 30 seconds. If more time is taken, some soil water will be absorbed by fingers and palms. If the rod crumbles under the pressure required for rolling and the soil cannot be rolled into a 1/8 in. (3 mm) rod, the soil is drier than the plastic limit. 4. If the soil can be rolled into a 1/8 in. (3 mm) rod, the soil is wetter than the plastic limit. # Ribbon Test to Determine Plastic Limit “the ribbon test involves digging soil to four inches deep and grasping a hand full of soil, squeeze it between the thumb and forefinger. If the soil forms a “ribbon” when squeezed, the soil is in condition for soil compaction to occur”. (Duiker, 1994). Determination of the plastic limit is independent of soil texture. If the soil is too granular to form a rod or a ribbon even when very moist, then it is not very susceptible to compaction and smearing. # Using Deep Tillage (Vertical tillage) Determine the Plastic Limit of your soil using one of the above procedures. Other observations or rules of thumb: If the soil makes a ball in your hand at the depth of tillage it's too wet to till. Or if shinny ribbons of soil peel off the equipment shanks as tilled, then the soil is too wet, or tillage is too deep. Once the depth and extent of the compacted zone is determined, there are several options for removing this yield robbing soil factor. Use a subsoiler or deep till with slots if the compacted layer is deeper than 12 inches. Set either implement to run about 1/2 to 1 inch below the bottom of the compacted layer. Sow a deep-rooted crop like alfalfa, sweet clover or tillage radish cover crop to break up the hard pan. # Deep Tillage with a Subsoiler For farmers that till, subsoil at least 12 inches deep when the soil is dry enough to shatter the hard pan. If the soil moisture is correct for every inch of subsoil shank depth, the soil should shatter out at a 45-degree angle or two inches per inch of depth (2:1). A lesser angle of shatter might indicate the soil is too wet to subsoil and may create a new tillage pan at the new deep tillage depth. In theory, dry soil breaks up and shatters much better then wetter, plastic soils (Harrigan, 1992). Avoid any secondary tillage operations in the fall after sub soiling. Dr. Gary Steinhart, Purdue University, says 80% of compaction is caused by the first trip over the field. If the soil is compacted by tillage and wheel traffic soon after subsoiling, the soil structure problem may be more severe than before the initial deep tillage. Staying out of the field just one more day in the spring could reduce compaction (Steinhart, 1979). # Deep tillage with Vertical Slot Tillage or Zone Tillage Another option to correct compaction before No-Till is to deep zone-till. In Don Schiefer’s book, Tillage in Transition, deep compaction from rutting or tilling soils that are too wet, is corrected by locating the depth of the tillage hardpan, determining its thickness, and tilling a narrow slot through the pan when the subsoil is damp, i.e. (damp: soil sticks together, but easily breaks apart with pressure). Schriefer recommends a zone builder to aerate the soil, improve drainage and strengthen soil structure. Zone tillage at the correct soil moisture will smear the subsoil and compact each side of the shank so there is a permanent crack in the subsoil. More recently, some agronomists refer to this tillage as vertical tillage. It is important to control traffic in vertical tillage to prevent wheel track axle loads from closing the subsoil slot, i.e. do not drive over the slots, if possible. It is also important to plant the crop near this slot to allow the crop roots to penetrate below the compacted soil tillage pan. The next crop can then follow the old root channels. This will help insure that the subsoil zone remains open, so roots can penetrate deeper for moisture and nutrients while remaining in an air-filled environment. With deep tillage, soil aeration, and controlled traffic: The roots replace the slots and keep the root channels and worm holes open for improved drainage into the subsoil. The narrow slots serve as future expansion zones for freezing and thawing forces to keep the zonetilled slot open. Microbial soil activity is improved due to aeration and a carbon food source (deep roots). Two years of deep slot tillage, followed by driving on soils only when it’s dry or the right moisture for tillage, should prevent soil compaction from occurring. Deep Slots ahead of soybeans on low wet ground without tile drainage “provided improved drainage compared to No-Till for soybean growth during the extraordinary wet years, such as the one encountered in 2004.” As a result, after 2 flooding events in the spring, the seed germination and plant stand at maturity was considerably higher on slots compared to the no till plot (Dierberger, 2005).

**Cultivating and Harvesting Willow for Basket Weaving and Home Décor**  

Willow has been a favored material for artisans for centuries, prized for its flexibility, strength, and the subtle beauty it brings to woven objects. Whether you are crafting functional baskets, sculptural pieces, or rustic home décor, understanding how to grow, maintain, and harvest willow is key to producing consistently high-quality weaving material.

---

### Choosing and Preparing the Site

Willow thrives in moist, well-drained soils and benefits from a location with full sun exposure. Before planting, clear the area of perennial weeds and grasses, as these can compete for nutrients and water. Loamy soils rich in organic matter are ideal, but willow is adaptable, tolerating heavier clays if drainage is adequate.

To prepare the soil, dig over the planting area to a depth of at least 30 cm, incorporating well-rotted compost or manure. This improves fertility and structure, encouraging strong, straight shoots. If your site is prone to drying out, consider creating shallow trenches or swales to help retain moisture, as consistent hydration supports vigorous growth.

---

### Planting and Establishment

Willow is typically propagated from hardwood cuttings taken during the dormant season. Cuttings of 20–30 cm in length and about the thickness of a pencil are ideal. Plant them directly into the prepared soil in late winter or very early spring, inserting two-thirds of the cutting below ground. Spacing depends on intended use: for basketry rods, closer spacing (about 25–30 cm apart) encourages tall, slender stems.

During the first growing season, keep the planting area weed-free and water regularly. Mulching with organic material helps conserve moisture and suppress weed growth.

---

### Pruning Cycles for Quality Rods

Consistent pruning is essential for producing the long, straight, and flexible rods valued in weaving. The most common system is **coppicing**, where all shoots are cut back to the base each winter after leaf fall. This stimulates a flush of uniform stems in spring.

After the first year of establishment, begin the annual coppice cycle. Use sharp, clean tools to make smooth cuts close to the stool (the base of the plant). Remove any damaged or crooked shoots, as these are less suitable for fine weaving.

For some decorative or structural projects, a **pollarding** method—cutting stems at a higher point—may be preferred, as it encourages branching at a set height. However, for basketry, coppicing generally yields the best weaving material.

---

### Managing Growth and Health

Willow responds well to generous watering, especially during dry spells, and benefits from a spring application of balanced organic fertilizer. Monitor for common pests such as willow aphids and rust; early intervention with organic controls helps maintain stem quality.

Regular thinning during the growing season can improve air circulation, reducing disease incidence. This also allows more light to reach developing stems, promoting even growth.

---

### Optimal Harvesting Seasons

For weaving purposes, willow is usually harvested during its dormant season—late autumn through winter—once the leaves have fallen and sap flow has slowed. Rods cut at this time are easier to handle, store, and prepare.

Harvest by cutting stems as close to the base as possible, grouping them by length and thickness. This sorting makes later weaving work more efficient and ensures consistency in the finished product. Avoid leaving cut rods in contact with damp ground for extended periods, as this can promote mold or premature sprouting.

---

### Storing and Preparing Willow

Freshly cut willow can be used immediately for certain projects, but more often it is dried for later use. Bundle rods tightly and store them upright in a cool, airy shed. When it’s time to weave, dried rods can be rehydrated by soaking in water—duration varies by thickness and species—to restore pliability.

Some artisans prefer to peel willow bark for a smoother finish, while others enjoy the natural texture and color variation it provides. Bark removal is easiest in spring, when sap rise loosens the fibers.

---

### Integrating Willow into Artisanal Work

Beyond traditional baskets, willow lends itself to lampshades, wall hangings, wreaths, and even small furniture frames. The natural curves and subtle hues of different willow varieties offer creative possibilities that synthetic materials rarely match. By mastering the cycle of soil preparation, pruning, and seasonal harvesting, you can ensure a steady supply of high-quality rods for your craft.

---

With attentive cultivation and a disciplined pruning and harvest routine, willow can become a renewable, sustainable source of artistic inspiration year after year—an enduring connection between the garden and the workshop.

polymers are reduced to their chemical building-blocks ( [ monomers

recycling normally being higher than that of mechanical recycling.  [82]  PET,

**Sustainable Interior Design Trends for Small Urban Apartments**  

In recent years, small urban apartments have become a canvas for creative, eco-conscious design. Limited square footage and the need for multifunctional spaces have encouraged residents to embrace sustainability not only as a lifestyle choice but as a practical solution to spatial challenges. By integrating eco-friendly materials, modular furniture, and strategic use of natural light, these interiors can become both stylish and efficient, all while reducing environmental impact.  

**Eco-Friendly Materials: A Foundation for Healthier Living**  
One of the most significant shifts in sustainable interior design is the prioritization of materials that are renewable, non-toxic, and responsibly sourced. Bamboo, cork, reclaimed wood, and recycled metal are increasingly popular for flooring, cabinetry, and decorative elements. These materials offer durability and unique aesthetic qualities while minimizing the carbon footprint associated with production. In textiles, organic cotton, hemp, and linen provide breathable, hypoallergenic options for upholstery, curtains, and bedding.  

For small apartments, using eco-friendly finishes can have a direct impact on indoor air quality. Low-VOC (volatile organic compound) paints and sealants reduce harmful emissions, making the space healthier for occupants. Additionally, incorporating natural fibers and untreated wood can create a warm, inviting environment without relying on synthetic materials that may degrade over time.  

**Modular Furniture: Maximizing Space and Functionality**  
Modular furniture has become a hallmark of sustainable urban living. Designed to adapt to changing needs, these pieces often serve multiple purposes—such as a sofa that converts into a bed, or a dining table that folds into a wall-mounted desk. This adaptability reduces the need to purchase additional items, lowering resource consumption and waste.  

Brands specializing in modular design are increasingly turning to sustainable manufacturing processes, using recycled components and minimizing packaging. For small apartments, modular systems also allow residents to reconfigure their layout as needed, extending the life of each piece and avoiding the disposable mentality often associated with fast furniture.  

Custom-built modular units can further optimize storage, integrating shelving, seating, and work areas into a single design. This not only saves space but also reduces clutter, which can make a small apartment feel more open and comfortable.  

**Natural Lighting: Enhancing Energy Efficiency and Well-Being**  
Harnessing natural light is a simple yet powerful way to improve sustainability in interior spaces. In small apartments, maximizing daylight can reduce reliance on artificial lighting, lowering energy consumption and utility costs. Large windows, strategically placed mirrors, and light-colored walls can help reflect and amplify sunlight throughout the space.  

Natural lighting also contributes to occupant well-being, supporting circadian rhythms and creating a more uplifting environment. Skylights, solar tubes, and glass partitions can be used creatively to bring sunlight into areas that might otherwise remain dim. For renters who cannot make structural changes, lightweight, sheer curtains allow light to penetrate while maintaining privacy.  

**Integrating Greenery and Passive Design Elements**  
Beyond materials and furniture, adding plants is an increasingly popular way to enhance sustainability in small apartments. Indoor greenery not only improves air quality but also adds a calming, biophilic element to the design. Compact vertical gardens, hanging planters, and window boxes are ideal for tight spaces.  

Passive design principles—such as positioning furniture to take advantage of cross-ventilation—can also play a role. By allowing fresh air to circulate naturally, residents can reduce the need for mechanical cooling and air purification systems. Combined with natural light, these strategies create a more self-sustaining interior environment.  

**Conclusion: A Holistic Approach to Urban Living**  
Sustainable interior design for small urban apartments is about more than aesthetics; it involves making mindful choices that balance style, function, and environmental responsibility. Eco-friendly materials ensure healthy indoor environments, modular furniture maximizes utility, and natural lighting reduces energy demands. Together, these elements create living spaces that are adaptable, resource-efficient, and aligned with the principles of sustainability—proving that even the smallest homes can have a big impact on the planet.  

By approaching design holistically, urban residents can transform compact apartments into vibrant, sustainable sanctuaries that meet the demands of modern life while respecting the environment.

**Blending Solar Shingles into Your Home’s Architectural Story**  

When homeowners think about adding solar to their rooftops, the conversation often revolves around efficiency, cost, and energy savings. But for many, the visual impact is equally important. Solar shingles—sometimes referred to as photovoltaic roof tiles—offer a way to generate renewable energy without the pronounced, elevated appearance of conventional rack-mounted panels. By replacing traditional roofing materials with integrated photovoltaic elements, these shingles create a seamless look that can complement existing architectural styles while meeting energy goals.  

**The Visual Appeal of Solar Shingles**  

Unlike traditional panels, which sit atop an existing roof, solar shingles are designed to mimic the size, shape, and color of standard roofing materials. This allows them to blend into the roofline, maintaining the home’s original silhouette. Manufacturers often offer variations in hue and texture to match common asphalt, slate, or clay tile appearances. For homeowners in neighborhoods with strict aesthetic guidelines or homeowners’ associations, this can be a decisive advantage. A consistent roof surface can preserve curb appeal, potentially boosting resale value and avoiding conflicts over visible modifications.  

**Architectural Compatibility**  

The integration of solar shingles works best when considered alongside the home’s architectural character. For example, a Colonial-style home with a symmetrical façade benefits from uniform, evenly laid shingles that do not disrupt the visual balance. Modernist designs, with clean lines and minimal ornamentation, can pair well with solar shingles that offer a sleek, monochromatic finish. Even historic properties can accommodate solar shingles if local regulations allow, as the low-profile design can respect the building’s proportions and detailing.  

Material choice plays a role here—some solar shingles are slightly thicker or have a distinct sheen compared to their non-solar counterparts. Thoughtful planning ensures that these differences enhance rather than detract from the overall look. This might mean replacing the entire roof surface for uniformity, or blending solar and non-solar shingles in patterns that align with architectural features.  

**Local Permitting Considerations**  

While solar shingles may sidestep certain aesthetic objections, they still fall under building and electrical codes. Local permitting processes vary widely: some municipalities treat solar shingles as both a roofing and electrical project, requiring dual inspections. In historic districts, design review boards may need to approve the appearance before work begins.  

Permitting timelines can be influenced by how the project is presented. A clear plan showing that the shingles will match or complement the existing roof can help expedite approvals. Documentation from the manufacturer regarding fire ratings, wind resistance, and waterproofing can also reassure officials that the installation meets or exceeds local safety standards.  

**Installation Planning for Seamless Integration**  

Because solar shingles replace traditional roofing, their installation often coincides with a roof replacement or major renovation. This timing allows homeowners to choose shingle styles and colors that best match the overall design. Coordinating with both a roofing contractor and a solar installer is critical; the former ensures proper weatherproofing and alignment, while the latter handles electrical connections and energy system integration.  

Some homeowners opt to install solar shingles only on the sunniest roof sections, using matching non-solar shingles elsewhere. This approach maintains uniformity while optimizing energy generation. However, partial installations should be carefully designed to avoid abrupt visual transitions between solar and non-solar areas.  

**Balancing Function and Form**  

Solar shingles represent a growing category in residential renewable energy solutions, appealing to those who value both performance and aesthetics. They offer a way to meet sustainability goals without introducing stark visual changes to a home’s exterior. By considering architectural style, color matching, and local permitting requirements early in the planning process, homeowners can achieve a harmonious integration that satisfies both energy needs and design preferences.  

In the end, the success of solar shingles lies in viewing them not just as an energy technology, but as a roofing material in their own right—one that must contribute to the home’s overall narrative, just as brickwork, siding, or landscaping does. Thoughtful integration ensures that the roof remains a cohesive, attractive feature while quietly producing clean energy for years to come.

By contrast, the RDE test has a broader range of parameters, each with ample margins allowed to cover a broad spectrum of driving possibilities. # TRIP SPECIFICATIONS RDE trips cover three types of operation: urban, rural, and motorway. **Greening the Tropics: The Urban Benefits of Tropical Ornamental Flora**  

Cities in tropical regions often face the dual challenge of maintaining livable, attractive environments while mitigating the impacts of rapid urbanization. One increasingly popular approach is the integration of ornamental tropical plants into public spaces, streetscapes, and residential gardens. Species such as hibiscus, frangipani, and bougainvillea not only lend vibrant color and character to urban areas but also contribute meaningfully to ecological health and comfort.  

### Aesthetic Appeal and Cultural Identity  

Ornamental tropical plants offer a visual richness that helps define the identity of a city. Hibiscus, with its large, showy blooms in shades from crimson to golden yellow, has long been associated with hospitality and warmth. Frangipani, known for its waxy, fragrant flowers, carries deep cultural symbolism in many tropical societies, often used in ceremonies and traditional garlands. Bougainvillea, with its cascades of papery bracts in vivid magenta, orange, or white, can transform walls, fences, and pergolas into living artworks.  

Such botanical accents do more than beautify—they create a sense of place. In neighborhoods where these plants are common, residents and visitors alike experience a visual continuity that reinforces local character and pride. Seasonal blooming cycles add dynamism to the urban landscape, marking transitions in climate and community life.  

### Biodiversity Enhancement  

Beyond their ornamental value, tropical flora can support urban biodiversity. Hibiscus shrubs, for example, attract pollinators such as butterflies and bees, while frangipani flowers are a nectar source for moths and certain species of bats. Bougainvillea, though less nectar-rich, provides shelter for small birds and insects within its dense, thorny branches.  

When planted in clusters or alongside native species, these ornamentals can form microhabitats that sustain a variety of organisms. This biodiversity, in turn, strengthens urban ecosystems, making them more resilient to environmental stressors such as heat waves or pest outbreaks. The presence of pollinators supports fruiting plants in nearby gardens, while birds help control insect populations.  

### Shade Creation and Climate Moderation  

In tropical cities, shade is not just a comfort—it is a necessity. Mature frangipani trees, with their wide-spreading branches, can provide generous canopy cover over sidewalks, playgrounds, and outdoor seating areas. Bougainvillea, when trained over trellises or pergolas, offers filtered shade that can cool patios and transit stops. Hibiscus, though smaller, can be part of layered plantings that reduce ground-level heat and glare.  

The cooling effect of shade from these plants can lower ambient temperatures in their immediate surroundings by several degrees. This contributes to reduced urban heat island intensity, potentially decreasing energy consumption for air conditioning in nearby buildings. In addition, shaded areas encourage outdoor social interaction, helping to knit communities together.  

### Low-Maintenance Landscaping  

Many tropical ornamentals are well-adapted to the climatic conditions of their native or adopted regions. Bougainvillea, for instance, thrives in full sun and tolerates periods of drought once established, making it suitable for water-conscious landscaping. Frangipani requires minimal pruning and can withstand poor soils, while hibiscus responds well to regular trimming and can be cultivated in containers for space-limited areas.  

Their adaptability means that urban planners and residents can achieve lasting visual and ecological benefits without excessive maintenance costs or resource inputs. Choosing species with low fertilizer and irrigation needs also aligns with broader sustainability goals.  

### Integrating Ornamentals into Urban Planning  

Successful integration of tropical ornamentals into cityscapes requires thoughtful planning. Selecting appropriate planting sites, ensuring compatibility with local infrastructure, and combining ornamentals with native vegetation can maximize benefits. In mixed-use developments, these plants can soften the lines of modern architecture, provide privacy screens, and delineate pedestrian zones. Public parks can incorporate them into themed gardens that celebrate regional botanical heritage.  

Community engagement plays a key role. When residents participate in planting and caring for ornamentals, they develop a stronger connection to their surroundings. Educational signage about the ecological roles of hibiscus, frangipani, and bougainvillea can further enhance appreciation and stewardship.  

### Conclusion  

Planting tropical ornamental flora in urban environments is more than an exercise in beautification—it is an investment in ecological vitality, cultural richness, and climate resilience. Hibiscus, frangipani, and bougainvillea, with their unique aesthetic qualities and environmental benefits, exemplify how thoughtful landscaping can transform tropical cities into greener, more livable spaces. By integrating these plants into public and private realms, urban areas can cultivate not just shade and biodiversity, but also a lasting sense of place that reflects both natural abundance and human creativity.

Translucent glass panes or walls can also be incorporated into spaces to add comfortable light that isn’t as bright light transmitted through clear glass. Every time you use your credit card, fees go to the bank that issued it. You can make sure this money is used to build a better world by finding a responsible credit card. ### Just as your bank decides how to use your deposits, so does the bank that issues your credit card decide how to use the credit card fees. If the issuer of your card is one of the US megabanks, then any fees you or merchants pay for your credit card purchases are being disproportionately loaned to or invested in the fossil fuel industry. Megabanks support the fossil fuel industry in two ways: - They loan money for fossil fuel projects - They invest money in fossil fuel companies ### Lending to fossil fuel projects To find out if the bank that issues your credit card is a **major lender** to fossil fuel projects, check the Banking on Climate Chaos report. This report lists nine US banks that together have loaned **more than $2 trillion** to the fossil fuel industry since the Paris Climate Agreement: | | | | | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | **Bank Rank** | **Bank Name** | **2023 lending and underwriting to fossil fuel industry (in billions)** | **Total lending and underwriting since Paris Agreement (in billions)** | | 1 | JPMorgan Chase | $ 40.875 | $ 430.926 | | 2 | Citibank | $ 30.268 | $ 396.331 | | 3 | Bank of America | $ 33.682 | $ 333.159 | | 5 | Wells Fargo | $ 30.378 | $ 296.247 | | 14 | Goldman Sachs | $ 18.818 | $ 184.927 | | 15 | Morgan Stanley | $ 19.104 | $ 183.547 | | 25 | PNC Financial Services | $ 12.149 | $ 108.312 | | 27 | Truist Financial | $ 14.232 | $ 105.352 | | 28 | US Bancorp | $ 12.779 | $ 97.274 | | | **Total for US megabanks** | **$212.29** | **$2,038.80** | Keep in mind that some of these banks may go by a shortened name on the back of a credit card. For example, US Bank owns Elan Financial, which issues credit cards for over 1300 banks and 300 credit unions – including some banks and credit unions that are otherwise sustainable. Regardless of which logo is on the front of a credit card, it is critical to find out which bank **issues** the credit card. ### Investing in fossil fuel companies To find out if the bank that issues your credit card is a **major investor** in fossil fuel projects, check the Investing in Climate Chaos database, published by the German environmental nonprofit Urgewald. **Urban Tree Planting Programs Drive Air Quality Gains and Cooler Cities**  

In an ambitious push to combat climate change impacts at the local level, several US cities have launched expansive urban tree planting initiatives aimed at reducing carbon dioxide concentrations, improving air quality, and enhancing urban livability. The programs, rolled out over the past two years, combine public funding, private partnerships, and grassroots community engagement to transform streetscapes, vacant lots, and underutilized public spaces into green corridors.  

**Funding and Partnerships**  
The scale of these greening efforts has been made possible through blended financing models. Municipal governments have allocated portions of their climate action budgets toward tree planting, often supplemented by federal environmental grants. In cities like Philadelphia and Sacramento, philanthropic organizations and corporate sponsors have contributed significant resources, citing both environmental stewardship and community health benefits. Tree nurseries, landscape architects, and local nonprofits have been contracted to supply and maintain plantings, ensuring both diversity in species selection and long-term care.  

In New York City, for example, the “Canopy 2030” program secured $50 million in municipal bonds, matched by $20 million from private donors. This funding structure allows for sustained planting schedules over a decade, rather than sporadic short-term campaigns. By establishing dedicated maintenance funds, cities aim to prevent the losses that can occur when newly planted trees fail due to insufficient care.  

**Community Engagement Strategies**  
A hallmark of these initiatives is the emphasis on neighborhood-level involvement. Organizers have found that engaging residents in planning and planting fosters a sense of ownership, which in turn improves survival rates for young trees.  

Volunteer planting days, educational workshops on tree care, and citizen science programs to track growth and health have become common features. In Detroit, for instance, residents use a mobile app to log observations about tree canopy density, pest activity, and seasonal changes. These data points feed into citywide monitoring systems, enabling rapid responses to emerging threats such as invasive species or drought stress.  

Schools have also been tapped to participate, integrating tree planting into science curricula. Students not only help plant saplings but also monitor soil conditions and measure tree growth, learning firsthand about ecological processes and the role of vegetation in carbon sequestration.  

**Environmental and Health Benefits**  
Early data from these programs show measurable improvements in air quality and temperature regulation. In Los Angeles, neighborhoods targeted for intensive planting have recorded average reductions of 2–3°F in summer daytime highs compared to similar areas without new canopy cover. These cooler temperatures reduce the strain on energy systems by lowering demand for air conditioning, indirectly cutting greenhouse gas emissions from power generation.  

Air quality sensors in Chicago’s “Green Grid” pilot area have detected a consistent drop in particulate matter and nitrogen dioxide levels over the past 18 months. While CO2 reductions are more challenging to measure directly at the neighborhood scale, researchers from local universities estimate that mature trees planted through the program could collectively sequester thousands of tons of carbon annually once the canopy reaches full size.  

Beyond climate and air quality metrics, biodiversity gains have been notable. Increased canopy cover has provided habitat for urban wildlife, from songbirds to pollinators, contributing to more resilient local ecosystems. Residents report more frequent sightings of species previously rare in dense city environments.  

**Challenges and Long-Term Outlook**  
Despite the successes, challenges remain. Securing adequate long-term funding for maintenance is critical, as young trees require years of care before they can withstand urban stresses independently. Urban planners are also grappling with ensuring equitable distribution of canopy cover, as historically underserved neighborhoods often have fewer trees and higher exposure to heat and pollution.  

Some cities are experimenting with advanced mapping tools to identify priority planting zones based on temperature data, air quality measurements, and socio-economic indicators. Integrating tree planting with other green infrastructure projects—such as rain gardens and permeable pavements—can amplify environmental benefits.  

As climate projections warn of hotter summers and more frequent extreme weather events, urban tree planting emerges as a multifaceted strategy. By blending ecological, economic, and social goals, these programs not only address immediate environmental challenges but also lay the groundwork for healthier, more resilient urban communities.  

The momentum behind these initiatives suggests that, with sustained investment and community support, urban forests could become a defining feature of American cities in the coming decades—cooling streets, cleaning air, and strengthening bonds between residents and their environment.

**Zero-length spring** is a term for a specially designed coil spring that
would exert zero force if it had zero length; if there were no constraint due
to the finite wire diameter of such a helical spring, it would have zero
length in the unstretched condition. That is, in a line graph of the spring's
force versus its length, the line passes through the origin. Obviously a coil
spring cannot contract to zero length, because at some point the coils touch
each other and the spring can't shorten any more.

## 1\. INTRODUCTION The rapid growth of society and the human population places a burden on natural resources. Natural resource consumption has been steadily rising \ [1\], and it has a big impact on pollution, environmental damage, and the depletion of natural resources \ [2\]. Construction and demolition waste (C&DW) generation has risen recently as a result of the construction industry's expansion \ [2\]. Another issue now is how to dispose of C&DW in an efficient and ecological manner \ [3\]. Lately, the global building industry has found it advantageous to produce sustainable concrete by substituting natural resources with waste products \ [4\]. Most experts agree that replacing natural aggregate in concrete with recycled aggregate produced from C&DW is an efficient solution to address both issues at once and contribute to sustainability \ [3\]. Also enhancing the long-term sustainability of cement-based construction can be achieved through the partial substitution of supplemental cementitious materials for cement. For example, Chen and Yang showed that cement paste containing no more than 20% Walnut shell ash has satisfying setting times and pozzolanicity in addition to a long-term compressive strength of 83 MPa, which it keeps for a maximum of one year \ [5\]. Chen _et al_. found that the best replacement amount of highly crosslinked thermoset plastic waste for sand in cement mortars with the highest compressive strength is 5%; above that, the compressive strength exhibits a steady fall \ [6\]. According to Chen _et al_., ternary blended concrete that included fly ash, silica fume, and a high dosage of used engine oil (5% by weight of cementitious materials) outperformed conventional concrete in terms of workability and compressive properties \ [7\]. Brick and ceramic waste fractions, which make up around 45% of the total C&DW are being produced at a faster rate globally as a result of more old structures being renovated and rebuilt \ [8\]. Currently, the ceramic industries generate enormous volumes of waste that have an adverse effect on the environment and create landfill issues. In 2015, the global output of ceramic tiles was over 12.4 billion square meters \ [4\]. Depending on where the raw materials came from, ceramic waste is divided into two groups. One group is created from waste-burnt ceramics produced by structural manufacturers of ceramics who manufacture products using only red pastes (roof tiles, bricks, and blocks). Another group includes waste-burnt ceramics created by stoneware ceramic products (wall, floor, and sanitary ware) \ [9\]. Elevated strength, resistance to wear, prolonged serviceability, chemically inert and non-toxic, heat and fire resistance, and electric resistance are all features of these ceramic waste products \ [10\]. Furthermore, because of the chemical composition of the ceramic waste and its low thermal expansion coefficient, concrete containing ceramic waste aggregate is resistant to high temperatures. Additionally, it was noted that the porous nature of ceramic aggregate concrete contributed to a noticeably low value of thermal conductivity in the concrete mixes made with ceramic aggregates \ [11\]. Ceramic waste is produced in large quantities, and its usage in concrete is advantageous since it makes use of its pozzolanic effectiveness to provide satisfying outcomes in terms of mechanical and durability performances. Additionally, it helps the environment by preventing the overuse of natural aggregate \ [10, 12\]. Since 60–75% of the volume of concrete is made up of aggregates, any decrease in the amount of natural aggregate used will have a major influence on the environment. In addition to the negative environmental effects of stone pits, noise, dust, vibrations, and the impact on rural areas, the consumption of non-renewable resources tends to significantly restrict their use. According to Shah and Huseien, Portland cement's energy consumption of 5.13 GJ/ton was more than four times higher than ceramic powder's waste, estimated at 1.12 GJ/ton. Moreover, Portland cement has a considerably larger greenhouse gas release (0.904 tons/ton) than waste ceramic powder (0.045 tons/ton), which is linked to its higher energy use, cost, and greenhouse gas emissions. When compared to a conventional mixture, the cement blended with ceramic materials generated fewer greenhouse gases, regardless of the replacement proportion. A reduction of more than 37% in greenhouse gas emissions occurs during the production of 1 ton of blended cement containing 40% waste ceramic powder, releasing 1 m3 of emissions \ [4\]. Chen _et al_. found that the recycling technique can lower carbon dioxide emissions by 8050–10750 kg, energy consumption by 2.87–4.13 billion MJ, and disposal expenses by HK$3250–9450 per ton of used engine oil, and therefore recycling used engine oil into concrete is a practical and environmentally friendly alternative \ [13, 14\]. Similar to the emission of greenhouse gases, the cost of cement manufacture was the greatest because of the excessive amount of energy consumed through the manufacture and the significant efforts requested to transfer the material. Shah and Huseien stated that the production cost of cement was 600 RM/ton in comparison to 170 RM/ton for waste ceramic powder. Furthermore, as the amount of ceramic fine aggregate substitution for the fine aggregates increased from 0 to 25, 50, 75, and 100%, respectively, the cost of the mortar specimens decreased from more than 380 to 372, 362, 351, and 341 RM/m3. A significant amount of cost was saved by substituting a large quantity of waste ceramic powder ( _i.e_., 40%) for the cement. When waste ceramic powder was substituted for cement in an increase of 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, and 60%, respectively, the cost of the binder was lowered from 380 to 358, 335, 317, 287, and 264 RM/m3. It was demonstrated that the use of ceramic powder waste as a binder in the mortar specimens contributed significantly to the production of sustainable products \ [4\]. Artificial aggregates have substantially bigger surface areas than natural aggregates because of their numerous corner angles and rough surfaces. The mechanical behavior of concrete materials is significantly influenced by the kind, shape, and grading of the aggregate. The relationship between concrete qualities and characteristics of ceramic aggregates, such as gradation, must, therefore, be rigorously studied \ [15\]. Numerous studies have been published recently to look into how the size of the aggregate affects the properties of concrete. According to Liu _et al_. \ [16\], it is best to create particles that are less than 10 mm, which is frequently the maximum of a ceramic tile's thickness, when using discarded ceramic to generate recycled coarse aggregate. Silva _et al_. \ [17\] reported that the aggregate's size influences the compressive strength, which becomes greater while utilizing finer aggregate because of the enhancement in the surface area of the aggregate particles, thus reducing bond stress in an aggregate-cement paste. According to Pitarch _et al_. \ [18\], recycled ceramic sanitary ware, red clay bricks, and tile, all had lower density values than natural limestone aggregates, and their water absorption rates ranged from 0.69 to 18.31% depending on the type of material and particle size. According to Ghorbani _et al_. \ [2\], the strength of concrete mixtures increased for all sizes of crushed concrete waste (CCW) when 25% of it was added. Mostly, lowering the maximum the aggregate size led to a little improvement in the concrete strength and durability for the same CCW inclusion ratio, with the exception of abrasion. Moreover, the findings of the resistance to freeze-thaw cycles showed that employing CCW rather than natural concrete aggregate can enhance the durability properties of concrete. Sobuz _et al_. \ [19\] noticed that the aggregate size of 12–20 mm in the recycled aggregate concrete mixtures displayed larger workability compared to the 5–12 mm aggregate mixtures. Conversely, recycled aggregate concrete with aggregate size of 5–12 mm had greater compressive strength and splitting tensile strength as well as a larger elastic modulus compared to the recycled aggregate concrete mixtures with aggregate size of 12–20 mm. Researchers are encouraged to employ ceramic waste instead of aggregate in concrete production due to its enormous generation and low consumption. After reviewing the previous studies, it was found that the studies that dealt with the replacement of coarse aggregate by ceramic waste aggregate at varying maximum aggregate sizes, coupled with the variation of substitution rates of ceramic waste aggregate in concrete in general, are limited. Thus, in order to assess ceramic waste's actual potential for substitution of aggregates in novel applications, this research aims to investigate the effect of variations in the maximum aggregate size of coarse ceramic aggregate at different levels of substitution of natural coarse aggregate. Accordingly, several concrete mixtures were made using different volumetric ratios of coarse ceramic waste, including (0%, 25%, 50%, and 75%), in three distinct size ranges (12.5 mm, 20 mm, and 25 mm), substituting natural coarse aggregate. The hardened density, compressive strength, splitting tensile strength, ultrasonic pulse velocity as well as absorption properties were evaluated.

**Advancements in Energy-Efficient Siphon Systems for Large-Scale Hydroelectric Power Plants**  

---

**Abstract**  
Recent innovations in siphon-based water conveyance systems have shown significant potential for improving the operational efficiency of large-scale hydroelectric power plants. By refining siphon intake structures and optimizing flow dynamics, engineers have achieved measurable gains in turbine performance, reduced cavitation risk, and minimized energy losses. This report examines the latest design methodologies, computational modeling strategies, and material advancements that contribute to maximizing water flow through massive intake structures, with a focus on scalability and integration into existing hydroelectric infrastructure.

---

**1. Introduction**  
Hydroelectric power generation relies on the controlled movement of water from reservoirs to turbines, where kinetic energy is converted into electricity. While penstocks and gravity-fed conduits are the most common delivery systems, siphon-based intake structures have emerged as viable alternatives in certain geographic and engineering contexts. These systems operate by creating a pressure differential that draws water over an elevation without the need for pumps, offering potential energy savings. However, scaling siphon technology to industrial capacities presents challenges in maintaining flow stability, minimizing hydraulic losses, and ensuring structural integrity under variable load conditions.

---

**2. Design Considerations for Large-Scale Siphon Systems**  

**2.1 Flow Optimization**  
The efficiency of a siphon system depends largely on its ability to maintain high volumetric throughput with minimal turbulence. Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) simulations have been instrumental in refining intake and outlet geometries to reduce eddy formation and boundary layer drag. Designs incorporating gradual curvature rather than sharp bends have demonstrated up to a 15% improvement in sustained flow rates [1].

**2.2 Cavitation Control**  
Cavitation, the formation and collapse of vapor bubbles within the flowing water, can cause damage to siphon walls and downstream turbines. Modern siphon designs incorporate venting systems and controlled pressure zones to mitigate cavitation risk. Materials such as high-density polyethylene (HDPE) liners and reinforced composites are increasingly used to resist cavitation-related erosion.

**2.3 Structural Stability**  
For large-scale applications, siphon structures must withstand hydrostatic pressures over extended spans. Reinforced concrete with embedded steel frameworks remains the standard, but modular composite panels have gained attention for their reduced installation time and improved corrosion resistance.

---

**3. Integration with Turbine Systems**  
The interface between the siphon outlet and turbine intake is critical for maximizing energy conversion efficiency. Smooth flow transition reduces velocity fluctuations and pressure drops, thereby improving turbine blade longevity and performance. Adjustable gate mechanisms and variable geometry diffusers allow operators to fine-tune flow based on seasonal water availability and grid demand.

---

**4. Energy Efficiency Gains**  
Field studies from hydroelectric facilities employing large-scale siphon intakes have reported efficiency gains in the range of 3–8% compared to conventional penstock systems under similar head conditions [2]. These gains are attributed to reduced auxiliary pumping requirements, lower frictional losses, and improved alignment between intake flow and turbine operating curves.

---

**5. Case Studies**  

**5.1 River Basin Facility A**  
A siphon intake spanning 120 meters was installed to replace aging penstocks. The system utilized dual bell-shaped intake hoods to streamline water entry and minimize debris ingress. Post-installation monitoring indicated a 6% increase in net power output and significant maintenance cost reductions.

**5.2 Coastal Hydroelectric Station B**  
Faced with limited elevation drop, engineers implemented a siphon system with integrated air management channels to sustain prime during tidal fluctuations. Turbine efficiency improved by 4%, and the system demonstrated resilience against saltwater corrosion through advanced composite materials.

---

**6. Future Directions**  
Emerging research focuses on adaptive siphon systems capable of real-time flow modulation based on predictive analytics. Integration of sensors for pressure, flow rate, and structural strain enables automated adjustments to intake geometry, promising further efficiency improvements. Additionally, hybrid systems combining siphon principles with low-head turbine designs could expand hydroelectric potential in regions with minimal elevation differences.

---

**7. Conclusion**  
Advancements in large-scale siphon technology offer hydroelectric operators new opportunities to optimize water conveyance and enhance turbine performance. Through refined geometries, improved materials, and intelligent control systems, siphon-based intake structures can contribute to greater energy efficiency, reduced operational costs, and extended infrastructure lifespans. Continued interdisciplinary collaboration between hydraulic engineers, materials scientists, and computational modelers will be key to unlocking the full potential of these systems.

**Shades of the Road: A Cultural History of Automotive Paint Colors**  

When the automobile first rolled onto public roads in the early 20th century, its color palette was dictated less by consumer choice than by manufacturing practicality. The Ford Model T, for example, was famously offered “in any color the customer wants, so long as it is black.” This was not a whimsical restriction; black paint dried faster and was more durable under the production methods of the time, enabling Ford’s assembly lines to operate with unprecedented speed. Yet even in those early days, the aesthetic dimension of car color began to capture public imagination, sowing the seeds for a century-long interplay between technology, fashion, and cultural identity on four wheels.  

By the 1920s and 1930s, advances in paint chemistry allowed automakers to expand their offerings beyond utilitarian blacks and dark greens. Nitrocellulose lacquer, a fast-drying paint that could be polished to a high gloss, made vibrant hues possible. Luxury brands such as Cadillac and Packard began introducing rich maroons, deep blues, and cream tones, aligning with the Art Deco movement’s emphasis on opulence and geometric elegance. Car color became a status symbol, a visual shorthand for wealth and sophistication.  

The post–World War II era ushered in a dramatic shift. The optimism of the 1950s was reflected in pastel palettes—mint green, baby blue, coral pink—mirroring trends in home appliances and consumer goods. These colors resonated with a burgeoning middle class eager to embrace modernity and express individuality. Technological improvements in enamel paints and the introduction of two-tone schemes allowed automakers to experiment with contrasts and accents, further personalizing the driving experience.  

The cultural revolutions of the 1960s and 1970s brought boldness to the fore. Muscle cars roared onto the scene in high-impact shades like “Plum Crazy” purple, “Grabber” orange, and electric lime green. These colors were a deliberate statement, connecting the car to youthful rebellion, rock music, and the counterculture’s embrace of self-expression. Metallic flakes became popular, adding depth and shimmer to paint finishes and enhancing the visual dynamism of car bodies under sunlight.  

By the 1980s, however, a more restrained aesthetic emerged. Economic uncertainty and conservative cultural currents influenced the rise of monochromatic schemes—silvers, whites, and muted blues—that conveyed professionalism and understated elegance. Paint technology continued to evolve, with polyurethane coatings offering improved durability and resistance to fading. Luxury imports from Europe often showcased these subtler tones, reinforcing their image as refined and cosmopolitan.  

The 1990s and early 2000s saw a renewed diversification of palettes, driven by globalization and the rise of niche markets. Advances in water-based paints reduced environmental impact, while pearlescent and chameleon finishes offered sophisticated visual effects. Automakers tapped into lifestyle marketing, associating colors with particular values: rugged earth tones for SUVs, sleek metallics for sports sedans, and vibrant primaries for compact urban cars. Consumer choice became a central selling point, with online configurators allowing buyers to preview their selections before purchase.  

In recent years, technology and culture have intersected in entirely new ways. Matte finishes, once rare, have become a fashionable statement, particularly among luxury and performance models. Digital design tools have enabled manufacturers to create complex, layered pigments that shift subtly under different lighting conditions. At the same time, cultural attitudes toward sustainability have influenced color trends: earthy neutrals and natural greens evoke environmental consciousness, while minimalist palettes align with a broader design movement toward simplicity and timelessness.  

Automotive paint colors today exist at the nexus of tradition and innovation. They are informed by over a century of shifting cultural moods, technological breakthroughs, and consumer desires. What began as a purely functional necessity has become a key element of automotive identity, a language in which drivers and manufacturers alike express personality, aspiration, and belonging. From the utilitarian black of the Model T to the iridescent finishes of modern electric vehicles, the road’s spectrum tells a story—not just of cars, but of the societies that build, buy, and cherish them.  

As trends continue to evolve, one constant remains: the car’s color is more than a surface treatment. It is a cultural artifact, reflecting the era’s values and the individual’s place within it. Whether subdued or flamboyant, automotive hues will keep marking time in shades and tones, painting history with every passing mile.

# Eco-Friendly Waterproofing for Hiking Gear: Beeswax and Silicone Solutions

When you’re out on the trail, reliable waterproofing can make the difference between a comfortable, enjoyable trek and a soggy, miserable ordeal. Many modern water-repellent sprays rely on fluorinated compounds, but there are time-tested alternatives that can keep your gear dry without introducing persistent chemicals into the environment. Two of the most effective options are beeswax-based treatments and silicone-based waterproofing products. In this post, we’ll explore how these work, what products to consider, and how to apply them correctly to different types of hiking gear.

---

## Beeswax-Based Waterproofing

**Why Beeswax Works**  
Beeswax is a natural wax produced by honeybees. Its hydrophobic properties create a barrier that repels moisture while allowing the underlying fabric to breathe. When applied to cotton, canvas, or leather, it penetrates the fibers and solidifies, making water bead off the surface.

**Recommended Products**  
- **Otter Wax Fabric Wax** – Made from beeswax and plant-based oils, ideal for canvas jackets, backpacks, and hats.  
- **Sno-Seal Original Beeswax Waterproofing** – Popular for leather boots, offering long-lasting protection without softening the leather excessively.

**Application Instructions**  
1. **Clean the Gear** – Remove dirt and debris with a damp cloth. Let the item dry completely.  
2. **Warm the Wax** – Beeswax can be firm at room temperature. Warm it slightly in your hands or by placing the tin in warm water (lid closed).  
3. **Apply Evenly** – Rub the wax into the fabric using firm, circular motions. Pay extra attention to seams and high-wear areas.  
4. **Heat-Set** – Use a hair dryer or heat gun on a low setting to melt the wax into the fibers. This ensures even distribution and better penetration.  
5. **Cure** – Let the item sit overnight before use. The wax will harden, forming a durable water-resistant layer.

**Best Uses**  
Beeswax treatments are best for natural fabrics and leather. They can darken lighter materials, so test on a small area first.

---

## Silicone-Based Waterproofing

**Why Silicone Works**  
Silicone forms a flexible, water-repellent coating over synthetic fibers like nylon and polyester. Unlike oils or waxes, it bonds well with synthetic surfaces without compromising flexibility.

**Recommended Products**  
- **Nikwax Tent & Gear SolarProof** – A water-based silicone treatment that adds water and UV resistance to synthetic fabrics.  
- **Gear Aid Seam Grip + WP** – A urethane-based sealant with silicone additives, excellent for sealing seams on tents and rain gear.  
- **Atsko Silicone Water-Guard** – A spray-on silicone treatment for boots, backpacks, and outerwear.

**Application Instructions**  
1. **Prep the Surface** – Clean gear thoroughly and allow it to dry.  
2. **Apply in a Well-Ventilated Area** – For sprays, hold the can about 6–8 inches from the surface and apply an even coat.  
3. **Work into Seams** – Use a small brush or sponge to ensure coverage in stitching and high-stress areas.  
4. **Drying Time** – Let the item dry for at least 24 hours before use. Some silicone products may require a second coat for maximum protection.

**Best Uses**  
Silicone-based treatments excel on synthetic hiking gear: tents, rain jackets, and technical backpacks. They don’t significantly alter the appearance or breathability of modern fabrics.

---

## Maintenance Tips

- **Reapply as Needed** – Beeswax coatings may need refreshing every season; silicone treatments can last longer but should be reapplied annually or after heavy use.  
- **Spot Treatment** – When only certain areas lose water repellency, treat those sections rather than the entire item.  
- **Store Properly** – Keep treated gear in a cool, dry place to prevent degradation of the waterproof layer.

---

## Final Thoughts

Choosing the right waterproofing method depends on your gear’s material and your environmental priorities. Beeswax-based products offer a natural, biodegradable solution for natural fibers, while silicone-based treatments provide strong, long-lasting protection for synthetics. By using these alternatives and following proper application techniques, you can keep your hiking gear performing at its best while reducing reliance on persistent chemical coatings.

Whether you’re prepping for a weekend backpacking trip or maintaining your everyday outdoor wear, these methods ensure you stay dry without compromising on sustainability or durability.

A thermocouple is a small copper rod that keeps gas from leaking into your
home when the pilot light goes out. When there is no flame to heat the
thermocouple, it cools down and shuts the gas valve on your appliance. A
faulty thermocouple can extinguish a pilot light or keep the pilot light from
igniting altogether. If you suspect there’s an issue with your thermocouple,
it’s best to contact the professionals.

Combined chlorine is the combination of organic nitrogen compounds and
chloramines, which are produced as a result of the reaction between chlorine
and ammonia. Chloramines are not as effective at disinfecting water as free
chlorine due to a lower oxidation potential. Due to the creation of
chloramines instead of free chlorine, ammonia is not desired product in the
water treatment process in the beginning, but may be added at the end of
treatment to create chloramines as a secondary disinfectant, which remains in
the system longer than chlorine, ensuring clean drinking water throughout the
distribution system.

**Turning Everyday Waste into Creative Home Projects**  

In a world where household waste can accumulate quickly, finding inventive ways to repurpose materials not only reduces landfill contributions but also adds personality and charm to your living space. By transforming items such as old newspapers, fabric scraps, glass jars, and metal cans into decorative and functional creations, you can cultivate a more sustainable lifestyle while enjoying hands-on, creative work.  

---

### 1. Old Newspapers: From Reading Material to Art and Utility  

Newspapers may seem destined for the recycling bin, but they can become the foundation for numerous projects. One popular option is paper weaving, where strips of newsprint are interlaced to form placemats, storage baskets, or even decorative wall hangings. For a rustic look, lightly brush the woven surface with diluted paint or tea to add warmth.  

Another use is papier-mâché, an age-old craft that transforms shredded newspaper and paste into bowls, masks, or sculptural accents. With a coat of paint or varnish, these creations can be surprisingly durable. Rolled newspaper sticks, bound together, make lightweight frames, trivets, and even small shelving units. The key lies in sealing the paper to protect it from moisture, ensuring longevity.  

---

### 2. Fabric Scraps: Patchwork Potential  

Fabric remnants—whether from worn-out clothing, old linens, or tailoring leftovers—offer endless possibilities. Patchwork cushions and quilts are classics, but smaller scraps can be stitched into coasters, bookmarks, or reusable gift wraps.  

Consider creating braided rag rugs by twisting and sewing strips of fabric into spirals. These rugs add color to a room, and their tactile quality brings warmth underfoot. Fabric scraps can also become organizers: stitch together rectangular pieces to form pockets that hang from a wooden dowel, perfect for storing mail, keys, or craft supplies.  

For those who enjoy wearable projects, fabric flowers made from layered scraps can embellish hats, bags, or jackets, giving new life to old accessories.  

---

### 3. Glass Jars: Storage and Illumination  

Glass jars, from sauce bottles to candle containers, are sturdy and endlessly reusable. They can serve as pantry storage for dry goods, spices, or homemade preserves. Decorating jars with paint pens or etching cream can turn them into personalized gifts.  

For ambiance, glass jars make excellent lanterns. Place tea lights or LED candles inside, and wrap the exterior with wire or twine for a rustic touch. Hanging several in a cluster creates a warm glow for patios or living rooms. Jars also function as mini terrariums—layer gravel, activated charcoal, soil, and small plants to bring greenery indoors without requiring much maintenance.  

---

### 4. Metal Cans: Industrial Chic  

Metal cans, once emptied and cleaned, lend themselves to both decorative and practical applications. Punching holes in the sides with a hammer and nail creates patterns that glow when a candle is placed inside, producing charming luminaries for evening gatherings.  

Cans can be repurposed into planters for herbs, succulents, or flowers. Painting them with weather-resistant enamel adds both color and protection. Larger cans serve as utensil holders in the kitchen or as desk organizers for pens, scissors, and other supplies.  

For a more ambitious project, multiple cans can be joined together—riveted or wired—to form modular storage units or even light fixtures. The metallic finish complements modern and industrial décor styles.  

---

### 5. Combining Materials for Unique Creations  

Mixing different salvaged materials can yield striking results. A lamp base crafted from stacked metal cans topped with a fabric scrap lampshade lined with newspaper collage can become a conversation piece. Similarly, glass jars with fabric-covered lids can store sewing notions or craft supplies, while woven newspaper baskets lined with cloth scraps blend sturdiness with softness.  

By experimenting with combinations, you can create items that are both functional and aesthetically pleasing, reflecting your personal taste while reducing waste.  

---

### Conclusion  

Repurposing everyday waste materials into decorative and functional home items is a rewarding way to engage with sustainability. Old newspapers, fabric scraps, glass jars, and metal cans each offer distinct textures, strengths, and creative potential. With a bit of imagination and basic crafting skills, these humble objects can be transformed into pieces that enrich your home environment.  

The process encourages resourcefulness, reduces the demand for new materials, and turns what might be discarded into something cherished. Whether you choose simple projects like jar lanterns or more elaborate undertakings like patchwork quilts, each creation becomes both a statement of style and a step toward mindful living.

Trawl abundance indices indicate that the relative abundance of Delta Smelt has declined substantially since the 1980s. The observed decline in Delta Smelt abundance generally is consistent with declines of other pelagic species (e.g., Longfin Smelt \[Spirinchus thaleichthys\], Threadfin Shad \[Dorosoma pentenense\], and juvenile Striped Bass \[Morone saxatilis\]) in the Delta (Sommer et al. 2007a; Baxter et al. 2010; Stompe et al. 2020). The CDFW FMWT Delta Smelt annual abundance index has been zero every year from 2018 through 2022 (Water Years \[WY\] 2019–2023), the lowest on record (Figure 6A-1). All CDFW relative abundance indices show a declining trend since the early 2000s. As previously noted, USFWS implemented a new smelt monitoring program in 2016, called the EDSM program. This new program is used to measure the abundance and distribution of all life stages of Delta Smelt using a generalized random tessellation stratified design. Delta Smelt population estimates are now derived from this survey, with abundance suggested to be several thousand fish or fewer in recent years (see Figure 6A-2 for 2022 as an example). Source: White 2022. Figure 6A-1. Time Series of the Fall Midwater Trawl Water Years 1967–2022 Abundance Index for Delta Smelt Source: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service 2022a. # Figure 6A-2. Abundance Estimates for Delta Smelt from Enhanced Delta Smelt Monitoring Program Phase 1, Weeks 13–18, Water Year 2022 The continued low spawning stock of Delta Smelt relative to historical numbers suggests the population would continue to be vulnerable to stochastic events and continued human-caused alteration of the Delta. As described in detail by CDFW (2021:10), the Experimental Release of Delta Smelt Project proposes to annually release up to 120,000 adult equivalents of surplus cultured Delta Smelt each year into a portion of the current range of the species for a three-year period (2021– 2024). For example, in WY 2023, nearly 44,000 marked Delta Smelt reared at the University of California, Davis Fish Conservation and Culture Laboratory were released into the Sacramento River at Rio Vista and the Sacramento Deep Water Ship Channel during late November and mid to late January (Columbia Basin Research, University of Washington 2023a). The purpose of the Experimental Release of Delta Smelt Project is to inform the feasibility and design of potential future supplementation efforts. The cultured Delta Smelt are propagated at the University of California Davis Fish Conservation and Culture Laboratory in Byron, California. Considerable progress has been made on estimating absolute abundance of Delta Smelt, including adults (Polansky et al. 2019). These estimates are affected by factors such as fish behavior and local habitat features, such as turbidity influencing catchability (Polansky et al. 2019:721–722). However, turbidity may only have limited effects on catchability according to a recent simulation analysis (Tobias 2021). The continued low spawning stock of Delta Smelt relative to historical estimates suggest the population continues to be vulnerable to key threats (described below), especially when these stressors are occurring in consecutive years (e.g., drought) or across sequential life stages (e.g., high water temperatures). The Summer Townet Survey (STN) and FMWT abundance indices for Delta Smelt have documented long-term declines, while the newer $2 0 \\mathrm { - m m }$ and SKT abundance index trends generally are consistent with the more recent trends shown by the older surveys (Figure 6A-3 and Figure 6A-4). During the period of record, Delta Smelt relative abundance has declined from peak levels observed during the 1970s. The STN and FMWT abundance indices declined rapidly during the early 1980s, increased somewhat during the 1990s, and then collapsed in the early 2000s. Since 2005, the STN and the FMWT have produced indices that reflect less year-to-year variation than their $2 0 \\mathrm { - m m }$ analog, but overall, the trends in both sets of indices are similar. The general distribution of Delta Smelt is well understood due to its limited geographic distribution (Moyle et al. 1992; Bennett 2005; Hobbs et al. 2006, 2007). Potentially suitable Delta Smelt habitat in the Delta is geographically limited, generally characterized by high turbidity and tidally influenced low-salinity conditions. Suitable spawning and migration habitat are occupied seasonally. In most years, surveys do not sample Delta Smelt at the fringes of their geographic distribution. Delta Smelt have been observed as far west as San Francisco Bay, as far north as Knights Landing on the Sacramento River, as far east as Woodbridge on the Mokelumne River and Stockton on the Calaveras River, and as far south as Mossdale on the San Joaquin River. This distribution represents a range of salinity from approximately 0 ppt to 20 ppt. However, most Delta Smelt observed in the extensively surveyed San Francisco Estuary have been collected from locations within the legal critical habitat delineation. In addition, all habitats known to be occupied year-round by Delta Smelt occur within the conditions defined in the critical habitat rule (59 FR 852). Each year, the distribution of Delta Smelt seasonally expands following first flush, when adults disperse in response to increased winter flows and associated increases in turbidity and decreases in water temperature. The annual range expansion of adult Delta Smelt extends up the Sacramento River to about Garcia Bend in the Pocket neighborhood of Sacramento, up the San Joaquin River from Antioch to areas near Stockton, up the lower Mokelumne River system, and west throughout Suisun Bay and Suisun Marsh. Some Delta Smelt seasonally and transiently occupy Old and Middle River (OMR) in the south Delta each year, but face a high risk of entrainment when they do (Grimaldo et al. 2009; Smith et al. 2020). Since 2010, several conceptual models (Interagency Ecological Program Management Analysis and Synthesis Team 2015) and empirical models (Thomson et al. 2010; Maunder and Deriso 2011; Miller et al. 2012; Rose et al. 2013a; Hamilton and Murphy 2018) have explored life cycle models for Delta Smelt to identify and describe the reasons behind the population decline. Some of these models have recreated a trend observed in abundance indices, but each model has applied different methodology and predictive covariates. Collectively, these modeling efforts generally support water temperature, water clarity, and prey availability as key factors limiting Delta Smelt populations; water diversions and predation may also have significant impacts. The threats discussed below may be directly or indirectly affected by water operations. All Delta Smelt life stages are vulnerable to entrainment at the south Delta export facilities. In general, Delta Smelt salvage increases when certain conditions occur, principally when adults move into the south Delta when turbidity exceeds 10 to 12 Nephelometric Turbidity Units (NTU) (Sommer et al. 2011; Bennett and Burau 2015), and with increasing net OMR flow reversal (i.e., more negative net OMR flows). Based on field and salvage data, Kimmerer (2008, 2011) calculated that from near 0 percent to 25 percent of the larval and juvenile population, and from 0 percent to nearly 40 percent of the adult population, can be entrained at the Central Valley Project (CVP) and State Water Project (SWP) facilities annually in years with periods of high exports. Methods to calculate proportional loss estimates have since been debated (Kimmerer 2011; Miller 2011) and work on entrainment estimation has continued (Smith 2019; Smith et al. 2020). Korman et al. (2021) provided a preliminary estimate of adult entrainment during 2002 of 35 percent, based on combined behaviordriven movement models and population dynamics models, which was more than double Kimmerer’s (2008) estimate of less than 15 percent. Modeling efforts suggest that entrainment losses have the potential to adversely affect the Delta Smelt population (Kimmerer 2011; Rose et al. 2013a, 2013b; Kimmerer and Rose 2018), although the recent modeling study by Smith et al. (2021) reported that a hypothetical change from the recent OMR flow management strategy (i.e., tidally averaged flows no more negative than -5,000 cubic feet per second \[cfs\]) to a hypothetical management strategy of 0 cfs flow gave a relatively limited 3.6 percent increase in probability of population growth. Data on population distribution (Murphy and Hamilton 2013) suggest that entrainment is likely to be at the low end of the estimated range in most years. As a result of investigations into entrainment loss, entrainment risk has been limited by restrictions on export pumping since 2008 (U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service 2008:280–282, 2019:40–49).

**Finding the Sweet Spot: Choosing the Best Washing Machine Water Temperature**  

When it comes to doing laundry, water temperature plays a bigger role than many people realize. It can influence how clean your clothes get, how long they last, and how much energy you use in the process. Striking the right balance between effective stain removal, fabric care, and energy efficiency starts with understanding the differences between cold, warm, and hot cycles — and how they interact with modern detergents and various fabric types.  

---

### Cold Water Cycles (20–30°C)  

Cold water is the most energy-efficient choice, as it avoids the electricity needed to heat water. It’s ideal for delicate fabrics like silk or wool, which can shrink or warp under higher temperatures. Advances in detergent formulation mean that many products now contain enzymes and surfactants specifically designed to work well in cooler temperatures, breaking down common stains without the need for heat.  

Cold cycles are also good for preventing color bleeding and fading in dyed fabrics. This makes them a go-to for bright colors, dark garments, and mixed loads where you want to avoid cross-color transfer. However, cold water may be less effective against oily residues or certain protein-based stains, which can set into fibers without the help of warmth.  

---

### Warm Water Cycles (30–40°C)  

Warm water offers a middle ground — gentle enough for most synthetic fabrics yet warm enough to help dissolve detergent more efficiently and loosen dirt. It’s particularly suited for man-made fibers like polyester blends, cotton-poly mixes, and everyday items such as t-shirts, bed linens, and towels.  

A warm cycle can improve cleaning performance on light to moderate stains without causing excessive shrinkage or fading. It’s also a good choice for garments worn close to the skin, where body oils and sweat can accumulate. For households looking to balance cleanliness with energy savings, warm water often provides the best compromise.  

---

### Hot Water Cycles (50–60°C and above)  

Hot water is most effective at breaking down heavy soil, grease, and certain microbes, making it the preferred choice for heavily stained items, kitchen linens, or bedding after illness. Cotton fabrics, especially whites, can handle hot cycles well, and the higher temperature can help maintain brightness by dissolving residues that cause dinginess over time.  

That said, hot water uses significantly more energy than cold or warm cycles. It can also cause shrinkage in natural fibers, weaken elastic materials, and fade colors faster. For these reasons, hot washes are best reserved for targeted loads rather than everyday laundry.  

---

### Detergent Performance and Temperature  

Modern detergents are formulated to work across a range of temperatures, but their enzyme activity can vary. Enzymes that break down protein-based stains (blood, sweat, food residues) often perform well in warm water but may be less active in very hot cycles. Conversely, some bleaching agents in powdered detergents activate better at higher temperatures, which can aid in whitening fabrics.  

Liquid detergents tend to dissolve quickly in cold water, while powders may require a bit more warmth to fully disperse. Reading the detergent label can help you match the product to your preferred temperature range for optimal results.  

---

### Practical Recommendations  

- **Cold (20–30°C):** Use for bright colors, darks, delicates, lightly soiled everyday wear.  
- **Warm (30–40°C):** Best for synthetic blends, moderate stains, regular household laundry.  
- **Hot (50–60°C+):** Reserve for heavily soiled whites, linens, or items requiring extra hygiene.  

Mixing these approaches within your weekly laundry routine can help reduce energy bills while keeping clothes looking their best. Always check garment care labels before adjusting temperatures, as some fabrics may have specific requirements.  

---

Choosing the right water temperature isn’t just about cleanliness — it’s about caring for your clothes and the environment. By understanding the strengths and limitations of each setting, you can make informed decisions that extend the life of your wardrobe, improve wash performance, and cut down on unnecessary energy use. In the end, a thoughtful approach to temperature selection can make your laundry both cleaner and greener.
